items.name: 递进
items.plain: 第6章和第7章的重点字面上都写着leverage，容易让人觉得在重复讲同一件事。虽然实际内容是递进的（第6章讲怎么成为债权人，第7章讲leverage用到什么程度），但章节重点的表述需要更清楚地体现这个区别。

problems.text: CH06 和 CH07 这两级的重点一样(都是「债权leverage」),相邻两级要不一样
level_focus写的是「债权leverage」，和CH07的「leverage巅峰」字面上重复了leverage这个核心词，容易被误判为同一主题
problems.fix: CH06的level_focus改为「身份转变」或「成为债权人」，强调的是从商人到银行家的跃升；CH07保持「leverage巅峰」或改为「leverage操作」，强调的是leverage的量化使用和威胁停贷案例

notes.text: 留存检查:第一个甜头在 5 秒,晚于原片的 0.2 秒

写前分析的反转验证:事实 F06（商人买市政官职很普遍）- 稿子里区分两种路径：普通大商人买地方官职爬社会阶梯（FS04）vs top银行家用国家债务leverage直接获得矿产垄断权和政治决策权（FS06-07），后者才是'creditor说了算但又不敢pull'的悖论级别、F07（Charles V 1522年财政极差Fugger威胁停贷）+ F20（Philip II破产Fugger巨亏）- 稿子里正面处理leverage的双刃剑：1522年leverage最大时Fugger确实能威胁停贷迫使还款（FS06），但到1557/1575 Philip II破产时Fugger已经借太多、不敢停贷、最终巨亏（FS08）。论点从'债主说了算'升级为'债主在debt restructuring那一刻说了算，但欠太多时反而被锁死'。 和反转结论相反(论点用F01/F05/F02/F03撑住债权leverage的权力面，用F10/F20撑住leverage的风险面（债主也会破产）。F06和F07不推翻论点而是丰富它：F06区分地方买官vs国家债务两种scale，F07+F20展示leverage从有效（1522威胁停贷）到失效（1557欠太多不敢停）的转折。结尾必须同时落'creditor那一栏'和'不敢pull the plug'两面，才和事实一致。)

rounds.summary: 蓝图整体结构扎实，从12岁学徒到债主的等级递进清晰，反转用Philip II破产事实撑住。唯一需要调整的是第6章和第7章的重点表述，让两章的区别在字面上更明显：一章讲成为债权人，一章讲leverage怎么用。

CH01.text:
[CH01 | 0:00-1:10 | 底层学徒通过具体场景第一次接触行会规则和官员腐败，理解违规的绝对后果]

You're twelve years old. Your hands are stained with indigo dye. Thirty years from now, you'll write a letter to the Holy Roman Emperor telling him: without me, you could never have worn that crown.

But today, you're scrubbing wool in your master's workshop. He calls you over. Points to a wooden crate. "See that mark? The guild seal. Only cloth with that seal can be sold in the market. No seal, the city watch confiscates it. Fines the seller everything they have."

You follow him to the city gate. A merchant approaches the guards. Doesn't open his cart. Just hands something to the officer — you can't see what. The officer waves him through. Doesn't check the goods. Doesn't ask questions.

Your master leans close. "Remember this. You'll need to learn it too."

The next day, you're at the market. A small vendor is selling fabric. No guild seal. The city watch grabs his bolts of cloth. Throws them on the cobblestones. Tramples them. "Guild rules," they say.

The vendor begs. Says he has children. The watch doesn't look at him.

You ask your master why no one helps. He says: "Stand on the wrong side once, your seven years here count for nothing."

Seven years as an apprentice. No wages. You sleep in his house. Eat at his table. Become part of his household. You're learning that the market isn't about making the best cloth. It's about knowing which seal to carry, which officer to pay, and when to stay silent.

One mistake, and you start over. If they let you start at all.

CH02.text:
[CH02 | 1:10-2:44 | 新人承接第一个高流险任务，通过commenda合伙看到不对等的风险分配，目睹家庭成员可被替换的残酷]

You're 19. Seven years done.

A Venetian merchant finds you. He has 300 ducats to buy Flemish cloth. You take it to Genoa, sell it, bring back the profit. Split: he takes three-quarters, you take one-quarter.

You ask why he takes more.

He says: "Because when the ship sinks, it's my money at the bottom. You just wasted three weeks."

This is commenda. Unilateral. He puts up all the capital and stays on land. You provide the labor and take the voyage. Pirates, storms, spoiled cargo—that's your risk. His money might vanish, but he goes home to his bed. Your body might not come back.

Your father did this.

Five years ago, he carried another merchant's wool to Pisa. The ship hit a storm off Livorno. The cargo sank. He sank with it. The merchant sent your mother a message: regrettable, but the contract included no death compensation.

Three months later, you saw that same merchant at the docks. He was signing a new commenda with a younger man. Same route. Same terms.

He just found a new traveler.

Your mother still wears black. You take this contract because one-quarter of the profit is 75 ducats. Seven years as an apprentice, you never held a single coin. This is the first money you'll call yours.

The ship might go down. But if you don't get on the ship, you stay an apprentice forever.

How much can you save if you keep doing this? How many voyages until you move up?

CH03.text:
[CH03 | 2:44-4:10 | 身份升级后收入明显增长，生活条件改善，但同时暴露在更高层级的威胁中]

You're 25. Six years as a journeyman.

Six voyages. You saved enough to stop traveling. Now you work in London, building wagons for a merchant house.

The pay is 4 pence a day. Sometimes 5 when they need you on a rush order.

That's triple what a journeyman in the countryside makes. It's more in a month than your father made in a year before that storm.

You rent a room above a tavern. Your own door. Your own key. You don't eat at the master's table anymore.

You buy a new pair of boots. Leather, not cloth. They cost 8 pence — two days' wages. You wear them to the guildhall when you deliver a wagon.

The purchasing power matters more than the number. After the plague, wages went up but grain prices stayed flat. Your 5 pence buys what 8 pence used to buy thirty years ago.

You're eating meat three times a week now. You send money home. Your mother writes back: she bought a goat.

But the Flemish merchants are undercutting prices. They're bringing in wagons built in Antwerp, selling them for 20% less. The guildhall is talking about petitioning the magistrate to block foreign goods.

One of the Flemish traders gets jumped outside the docks. Two broken ribs. No one saw who did it.

The guild masters say it's about protecting English craftsmen. You know what it really is: they don't want competition cutting into their margins.

You keep your head down. You're making good money, but you're not protected yet. You're not a master. If the guild decides you're working with the wrong people, they can blacklist you. No one hires a blacklisted journeyman.

How long do you need to save to become a master? How much does it cost to buy your way into the guild?

CH04.text:
[CH04 | 4:10-5:51 | 成为垄断链条中的一环，获得定价权但导致平民受损，权力方对伤亡虚无化]

You're 30. Five years of commenda voyages, six years of journeyman wages, and a loan from a Florentine banker. You've saved 60 days' worth of wages. About 15 weeks of income. That's what it costs to become a master.

You present your masterpiece to the guild examiners. A bolt of cloth dyed with kermes, edges finished with Flemish technique. They inspect the weave. They check the color against guild standards. One examiner nods. The other writes your name in the register.

You pay the fee. 60 days of work, gone in one transaction.

But now you're on the other side of the door.

The guild hall, two weeks later. Thirteen master cloth merchants sitting around an oak table. You're the newest one. The oldest master, Francesco, runs the meeting.

"The Genoese are undercutting us," he says. "Selling Flemish wool at 8 shillings per yard when our rate is 10."

"They're not guild members," another master says. "We can stop them."

Francesco looks at you. "The city watch enforces guild regulations. Non-members caught trading in our territory—goods confiscated, fines, permanent ban from the market. Agreed?"

You nod. This is what you paid for.

The vote is unanimous.

One week later, a Genoese trader sets up in the marketplace. He's selling the same Flemish wool you sell, but at 8 shillings. By noon, he has a line of customers.

By afternoon, the city watch arrives. They don't ask questions. They confiscate his goods, load them onto a cart, and escort him to the city gate. The guild secretary records it: "Unauthorized trading by non-member. Goods seized, trader expelled."

The customers who were in line go back to buying from you and the other twelve masters. At 10 shillings per yard.

Francesco calls another meeting.

"Prices are too low," he says. "We're competing against each other. We should all raise to 12 shillings."

You do the math in your head. 20% increase. Your margin goes from thin to comfortable.

"The tailors will complain," someone says.

"Let them," Francesco says.

The vote passes. Twelve shillings per yard, effective immediately.

The complaints start within days. A tailor comes to your shop. "Twelve shillings?" he says. "I can't charge my customers enough to cover that. A gentleman's doublet now costs an extra 3 shillings."

You tell him what Francesco told you to say: "Prices reflect the quality of guild-certified cloth."

The tailor leaves. He has no choice. Guild-certified cloth is the only cloth the city watch allows in the market.

More complaints come in. Shopkeepers. Tailors. Even a minor nobleman's steward, saying the household clothing budget can't keep up.

Someone takes it to the city magistrate.

You hear about the meeting later. A group of tailors, a few shopkeepers, standing in the magistrate's office. They present their case: prices have gone up 20%, it's hurting their businesses, customers can't afford new clothes.

The magistrate listens. Then he says: "This is an internal guild matter. I have no authority to interfere with guild pricing."

The tailors leave. Nothing changes.

You find out why a month later. Francesco mentions it casually over wine. "The magistrate receives 2,000 florins a year from the guild. Consulting fees, officially. He's been on the list for three years."

You don't ask what the consulting is for. You already know.

Your income doubles that year. The price stays at 12 shillings. The complaints stop—not because people are happy, but because complaining doesn't do anything.

You bought your way into the guild. The guild gave you the power to set prices. The city watch enforces it. The magistrate looks the other way.

The tailors raise their prices. Their customers pay more for the same doublet. A apprentice cobbler's family buys one new shirt this year instead of two.

You don't see them. You see your account book. The numbers go up.

This is what a master does. You don't compete. You control.

But how long does this last? What happens if someone doesn't pay? What happens if you're the one who owes?

CH05.text:
[CH05 | 5:51-7:48 | 目睹同级别人物因债务崩溃的完整过程，理解信用体系的死亡线和破产的社会性死亡]

You're 35. Three apprentices. Two journeymen. Your workshop makes more in a month than your father made in three years.

One morning the city square fills with people. You push through the crowd.

A merchant you know is tied to a wooden platform. Two years ago you drank with him at the guildhall. Now the city crier stands next to him holding a scroll.

The crier reads. Loud enough for everyone to hear.

Eight thousand florins. Twelve creditors. Three months on the run before they caught him in Antwerp.

The crowd listens. Silent at first.

Then the auctioning starts. His wool bales. His looms. His carts. His workshop lease. The furniture from his house. Everything laid out in the square.

City watch stands in a circle. No one interferes.

A woman in the crowd yells "thief." A boy throws a rotting cabbage. It hits the platform. No one stops him.

The auctioneer counts. Five thousand florins total. He still owes three thousand.

The crier announces the sentence. Debtors' prison. Until his family pays the rest or the creditors agree to release him.

They untie him. Drag him toward the prison gate. He doesn't fight. Doesn't speak.

You later hear he stayed there three years.

In Florence the law is worse. Bankruptcy means permanent exile. Not just you. Your children. Your children's children. They strip your citizenship. You can never come back.

They call it eiectio a civitate. Ejection from the city. Forever.

You think about your own accounts. You owe six creditors. Smaller amounts. But if one deal goes wrong. If one shipment sinks. If one duke decides not to pay.

You could be the one on that platform.

The difference between him and you isn't skill. It's one bad month. One delayed payment. One creditor who decides to call it in.

You stop drinking with other merchants. You stop talking about debts. You start keeping two sets of books. One for the guild. One for yourself.

Trust is expensive. Bankruptcy is permanent.

How do you avoid this? Is there a level where debt doesn't destroy you? Where you're the one holding the paper instead of owing it?

CH06.text:
[CH06 | 7:48-9:53 | 身份彻底改变成为借钱给统治者的债主，债务规模和抵押物等级跿升，但信任瓦解和家庭牺牲]

You're 45. You don't trade anymore.

You have twelve agents. Venice, Antwerp, Lyon, Augsburg, Seville, Bruges, London, Frankfurt, Nuremberg, Genoa, Florence, Lisbon. Each one manages a portfolio. Each one sends you coded letters twice a month.

Your business now is lending to people who don't pay back on time. Dukes. Princes. Sometimes kings.

1537. Archduke Ferdinand of Austria needs 83,000 florins for military equipment. He sends a representative to your Augsburg office. The rate is 14% annually. You lend it.

Not because you trust him. Because you know his brother Charles V already owes another banking house over a million florins. If Ferdinand defaults, Charles will cover it. If Charles defaults, you're holding collateral on two kingdoms.

The math is simple. The risk isn't.

1519. Charles V wants to become Holy Roman Emperor. The election costs money. A lot of money. Total campaign budget: 850,000 florins. Your house provides 543,000. That's 64% of what it takes to buy the most powerful title in Europe.

You're not funding a campaign. You're buying leverage.

When he wins, you don't get paid back in cash. You get something better. Mining rights. Guadalcanal silver mines in Spain. Almadén mercury mines. Monopoly extraction contracts. The mines produce more than the loan amount every three years. As long as Charles stays emperor, you keep the rights.

You're not a merchant anymore. You're a creditor to the throne.

But you're paying for it in other ways.

1542. Your daughter's betrothal feast. You're in Antwerp negotiating a 300,000 florin loan restructure with a duke who's three years overdue. You send a letter. You send a gift. You don't go home.

She writes you once. You don't open it for two months.

1548. Your mother dies. You're in Venice. A prince's repayment is five weeks late and if he defaults, four other contracts collapse. You stay until he pays. You miss the funeral.

Your brother buries her. He doesn't write to tell you. You find out from an agent's report three months later.

You stop going to family events. You stop explaining why. After a while, they stop inviting you.

This is the cost of operating at this scale. You can't trust anyone to handle these negotiations. One mistake, one leaked number, one agent who switches sides, and you lose everything.

And the hardest part? You're right not to trust them.

1549. One of your partners. You lent him 20,000 florins for a Venice-London textile route. Reliable man. Ten years of clean trades. Then someone tells you he's negotiating to resell the shipment to your competitor before it even docks. Undercutting your price. Using your money to fund it.

You have no proof. Just a letter from an agent in Bruges. Just a rumor from a dock worker who might be lying.

But at this level, you can't wait for proof. You cut his credit line. Immediately. No warning. No explanation.

Three months later, he's bankrupt. His family loses their house. His son's apprenticeship gets cancelled because he can't pay the guild fee.

Six months later, you find out the rumor was false. A competitor planted it to destabilize your network. Your partner was clean.

You don't apologize. You can't. Apologies are admissions. Admissions are weaknesses. Weaknesses are fatal.

You have everything you thought you wanted at 19. Twelve cities. Mining rights. Kings who need you.

And you can't trust a single person in any of them.

Next question: How much leverage can you actually have over a king? What happens when the debt gets so large that he can't possibly pay it back?

CH07.text:
[CH07 | 9:53-11:26 | 展示债权帝国的量化规模，债主与国王的leverage在巅峰时刻的具体表现]

You're 50.

You need to understand the scale. When Charles V dies, his son Philip II inherits 20 million ducats in debt. Your family holds a major portion of it.

1539. Your accounting books show Charles V owes you 1.25 million florins on Spanish revenues alone. That's not counting Antwerp, not counting Lyon, not counting the mining contracts.

Most kingdoms collect 1 to 2 million ducats a year in total revenue. Charles owes you more than an entire kingdom makes in a year. Several kingdoms, actually.

This is the power. Not the mines. Not the agents. The debt itself.

1522. Charles's credit is so bad he can't borrow from anyone else. Your uncle Jakob writes him a letter. April 24, 1523. It says: "It is well known that Your Imperial Majesty could not have acquired the Roman Crown without me."

Not a suggestion. A statement. No pleasantries. No apologies.

The letter continues: immediate repayment required.

Charles pays. Not all of it. Enough.

That's leverage. When the emperor of half of Europe pays because you wrote a letter.

But here's what Jakob understood and what you're beginning to see: leverage only works up to a point.

If he owes you 100,000, you own him. If he owes you 1 million, you still own him. If he owes you 10 million, you're partners. If he owes you 20 million, he owns you.

Because if he can't pay, you can't collect. If you stop lending, he collapses. If he collapses, your 20 million becomes zero.

Jakob's letter worked in 1522 because Charles could still pay. The debt was large but not impossible.

You're past that point now.

Next question: What happens when your biggest debtor declares bankruptcy?

CH08.text:
[CH08 | 11:26-12:13 | 权力彻底反转，最大债务人破产，债主的leverage瞬间失效，从能威胁国王到被锁死的状态]

You're 55.

1557. Philip II, King of Spain, declares bankruptcy.

He owes you 1,660,809 ducats. Plus the silver shipment he "temporarily requisitioned" three years ago — still sitting in the royal treasury. 762,262 crowns' worth.

You think you can do what Jakob did in 1522. Threaten to stop. Force repayment.

But this time is different.

Philip owes too much. If you stop lending and he defaults completely, your 2 million ducats are gone forever.

So you can't stop. You keep lending. You keep waiting. You keep hoping he'll pay back something.

1575. He declares bankruptcy again.

1576. Antwerp is sacked. Your branch office burns. Account books destroyed.

You once wrote to an emperor: "Without me, Your Majesty could never have obtained that crown."

Now you live in a fortified house in Augsburg. You don't leave. You don't see creditors. You don't let the rest of the family know how much you've lost.

You own IOUs that will never be repaid. And a house you're afraid to leave.

The kid with indigo-stained hands became the man who could decide which kings wore crowns.

And then became the man who couldn't collect.

But does the system stop when you fall?

CH09.text:
[CH09 | 12:13-13:00 | 系统循环确认，前一代债主破产后下一代已在崛起，街角永远有新学徒，回扣开头]

No.

Two hundred years before you, there were the Peruzzi. They lent to Edward III of England. He borrowed. He borrowed more. He couldn't pay.

1340s. The Peruzzi and Bardi collapse. Total loss: 1,365,000 florins.

Fifty years later, in Florence, a new banking house opens. The Medici. 1397.

They learned from the Peruzzi's mistake. They made new ones.

And somewhere in Augsburg right now, there's a twelve-year-old boy. Hands stained with indigo dye. Watching a merchant at the city gate. Learning which city watch takes bribes.

He doesn't know that in thirty years, he'll write a letter to an emperor.

He doesn't know that in forty years, a king will owe him so much he can't ask for it back.

Next time you sit in a meeting, look at the balance sheet.

The most important person isn't the one with the biggest title.

It's the name in the creditor column who can't pull the plug.

angles.belief: 中世纪商人靠聪明的买卖赚钱
angles.claim: 他们真正的生意是买政治保护和行会垄断权，交易只是执行
angles.one_line: 商人卖的不是货，是通行证和禁令
angles.key_fact: 需查：行会商人对非成员的排斥条款与处罚权力；[R4]提到行会商人「tyrannized over craftsmen」但需要具体的准入限制和罚金数据
angles.why_watch: 发现「自由贸易」在中世纪根本不存在，买卖权本身就是商品
angles.risk: 关键证据是行会内部规则和执行记录，可能难找到量化数据；框架要求的「暴力」在行会主要是经济排斥而非物理暴力；结尾的「监狱-循环」在商人题材里不成立，只能改成「行会席位世袭或转卖」

angles.belief: 商人等级是按财富和经验分的
angles.claim: 等级其实是风险分配机制：行脚商人吃全部死亡率，行会老爷只出本金
angles.one_line: 层级不是晋升阶梯，是谁去死的分工表
angles.key_fact: [R1]和[R5]都提到商人需要travel和面对piracy/war，但需查：中世纪长途贸易中小商贩的死亡率或失败率 vs 委托贸易的行会商人损失比例；需查：commenda等合伙制里风险和利润的具体分配比例
angles.why_watch: 以为看的是「如何成为大商人」，其实看到的是「谁被设计成垫脚石」
angles.risk: 中世纪商人死亡率数据可能只有零散记录；风险分配确实存在但可能没有「暴力-政商」那么极端的对比；框架要求的「街角永远有下一个孩子」在学徒制里勉强能对应但动机不同

angles.belief: 商人和贵族政治是两个世界
angles.claim: 顶层商人的日常工作就是政治：他们放贷给国王、买贵族头衔、决定战争借款
angles.one_line: 最有钱的商人不再做生意，他们成为政权本身的债主和股东
angles.key_fact: 需查：美第奇、富格尔等银行家族给王室的贷款规模与对应的政治特权（垄断权、税收权、封号）；需查：这些贷款占国家收入或战争开支的比例
angles.why_watch: 发现「资本主义」不是从商业开始，是从商人买下政府开始的
angles.risk: 美第奇和富格尔的故事太有名，观众可能已经知道；这个角度在「层级叙事」里只能讲最顶层，缺少逐层递进；框架要求的「终局-监狱」完全不适用，顶层商人的结局是家族衰落或被国王赖账，不是被捕

title.final_title: Every Level of a Medieval Merchant
title.viewer_question: 中世纪商人从最底层到最高层是什么样的？每一级做什么、赚多少、付出什么代价？最顶层的商人有多大权力？
title.expected_answer_direction: 期待看到从学徒到富商的完整路径，每一级的生活细节、收入增长、社会地位提升

protagonist.who: 中世纪欧洲的商人（从12岁学徒开始，经历apprentice→journeyman→master→merchant→banker的完整路径）
protagonist.era: 中世纪晚期到文艺复兴早期（约1300-1550）
protagonist.place: 欧洲商业城市（主要是意大利佛罗伦萨、德国奥格斯堡、英国伦敦、法国里昂等贸易中心）
protagonist.source_role: 原片主角是墨西哥卡特尔成员（男性），从最底层望风者到最高层头目
protagonist.mapping: 原片'组织'→本题'行会/商业网络'；原片'地盘'→本题'市场垄断/贸易路线'；原片'暴力'→本题'经济leverage/债权'；原片'警察'→本题'城市官员/国王'；称呼都是第二人称'你'不变

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 中世纪商人就是做买卖的生意人，靠卖货赚钱，和国王贵族是两个世界
thesis_card.truth: 顶级商人（Fugger/Medici级别）不再靠卖货，他们成为政权的债主：借钱给国王打仗、用债务换矿产垄断权和政治决策权，国王欠他们的钱比整个王国的年收入还多。但债主不等于主人——国王可以赖账、破产、没收财产，债权leverage在debt restructuring那一刻最大，之后随时可能灰飞烟灭
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 中世纪商人的最高级不是卖得最多的人，而是让国王欠你的钱多到还不起、但你又不敢停贷的人
thesis_card.ending_landing: 今天谁的presentation最重要？不是title最大的那个人，而是资产负债表creditor那一栏里写着名字、但又不敢pull the plug的人。Peruzzi破产了，Fugger在Philip II破产时巨亏，但下一个Medici已经在路上。街角永远有新的12岁学徒，手上沾着靛蓝染料，不知道30年后他会写一封信告诉皇帝：没有我，你不可能戴上那顶王冠。也不知道40年后国王会欠他的钱多到他不敢要回来。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论是'暴力只是表层，真正支撑它的是政商网络；头目只是可替换零件，系统永续'。本题结论是'贸易只是表层，真正的权力是debt leverage；但leverage是双刃剑——国王欠你钱多到你说了算，也多到你不敢让他还不起；商人个体可以破产（Peruzzi/Bardi/Fugger都亏了），但债权-政权共生关系永续'。核心逻辑相同（表层vs深层、个人vs系统永续），但增加了leverage的双刃剑悖论。
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为中世纪商人靠卖货赚钱、和王权是两个世界，实际顶级商人用债务leverage控制政权（F05: Jakob Fugger 1523年写信'没有我陛下不可能获得罗马皇冠'），但leverage到极限时债主反而被锁死（F20: Philip II破产Fugger巨亏）
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样是欠债不还：普通商人欠钱会被公开羞辱、财产没收、关进债务人监狱直到还清（F17: Veckinchusen被关3年破产）；国王欠Fugger 1.66 million ducats却能继续借、还能赖账破产、Fugger不敢停贷怕血本无归（F20）
thesis_card.boundary: 论点只适用于top-tier银行家族（Fugger/Medici/Peruzzi级别）在15-16世纪欧洲王权财政危机期的债权leverage；不适用于地方行会商人（他们的权力来自市场垄断F08，不是国家债务）或普通贸易商（F16: 中型商人利润率14-17%、现金流紧张）。Leverage的双刃剑悖论：国王欠你越多你权力越大，但也越不敢让他还不起，因为他破产你就全亏了。

facts.content: 15世纪末Medina del Campo市议会regidor职位从7个增至13个，新增职位主要被商人购买；1559-76年13个regidor中8个是商人
facts.source: bibliotecadigital.jcyl.es

facts.content: Charles V 1522年财政极差'credit如此之坏'，Fugger威胁停贷才迫使还款
facts.source: So schlecht war der Credit des Kaisers im Jahre 1522

facts.content: 行会规章明确禁止非成员交易、没收货物、罚款，需要市长介入执行
facts.source: 写前论点调研

facts.content: 学徒中40-60%能成为master
facts.source: 写前论点调研

facts.content: Peruzzi和Bardi被Edward III赖账导致破产：Edward III欠Bardi 180,000 marks、欠Peruzzi 135,000 marks（每mark等于4.5金弗罗林），总计约1,365,000弗罗林；两家公司在1340s破产
facts.source: Digital Silk Road Project, Toyo Bunko

facts.content: 学徒期通常7年（部分行业2-10年不等：厨师2年、木匠/制桶匠4年、皮毛商5年、铁匠/裁缝6年、屠夫/刀匠8年、金匠/锁匠10年）
facts.source: Dictionnaire Historique, French medieval guilds

facts.content: 学徒通常从12-14岁开始，成为学徒后成为师傅家庭的一员，师傅提供食宿、教授技艺但不支付工资
facts.source: English Gilds archive, University of Michigan

facts.content: 14世纪journeyman（熟练工）日工资：普通木匠3便士/天、高级木匠3-4便士/天、伦敦可达4-5便士/天；泥瓦匠同等级；双人锯木工一组共7便士/天；特殊技能或强制征用时乡村可达4-5便士/天
facts.source: James E. Thorold Rogers, Six Centuries of Work and Wages

facts.content: 13世纪成为master需向行会支付入会费（Paris鞋匠：16苏帕里西斯现金，相当于现代25法郎购买力，另每年交32苏）；15世纪后期费用大幅上涨：15世纪平均需60个工作日工资（约15周），16-17世纪平均158天工资（约31周），18世纪达382天工资（约76周）
facts.source: Guild mastership fees table, European guild studies

facts.content: 海上贸易风险包括海盗、风暴、货损；commenda合伙制中，出资者（stans）承担全部财产损失风险但留在陆地，旅行商人（procertans）提供劳动和航海风险
facts.source: Italian medieval commenda contracts

facts.content: 15世纪中型商人年贸易额：英格兰羊毛商人Thomas Heritage 1495-1520年间主要交易wool，利润率极薄、现金流持续紧张；15世纪中期Johann Rosenkrantz在英格兰购买7,000莱茵弗罗林的布料委托销售，净利润约1,000弗罗林（14-17%年利润率）
facts.source: A Country Merchant 1495-1520 study & German merchant records

facts.content: 破产商人会被债主逮捕并关进债务人监狱，直到清偿债务或债主满意为止；佛罗伦萨破产法规定破产者及其后代永久驱逐出城（eiectio a civitate）、剥夺公民身份；商人Hildebrand Veckinchusen在布鲁日被捕后监禁至1425年（长达3年），导致商业网络崩溃、企业破产
facts.source: Bruges debt imprisonment records & Florence bankruptcy statutes

facts.content: Medici银行由Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici于1397年建立，在Peruzzi/Bardi 1340s破产后约50年崛起
facts.source: Wikipedia & historical banking records

facts.content: commenda合伙制利润分配：unilateral commenda（单边）中出资者提供全部资本、旅行商人提供劳动，利润分配3/4给出资者、1/4给旅行者；bilateral commenda（双边）中出资者和旅行者各出一半资本，利润对半分；出资者承担全部财产损失风险，旅行商人承担航海和人身风险
facts.source: Italian commenda contracts, Venice & Genoa

facts.slot: Fugger家族在Philip II破产中的损失
facts.content: 1557年Philip II破产时，Fugger家族在西班牙的债权达1,660,809 ducats（不含荷兰债权），加上被扣押的银矿银子价值762,262 crowns（含14%利息）；1575年Philip II第二次破产后安特卫普被洗劫（1576年），Fugger business进入衰退期
facts.source: German historical archives on Fugger family

facts.content: 14世纪晚期起，journeyman要成为master必须通过严格考试：制作一件'masterpiece'（杰作）证明技艺精通，并支付高额费用；多数情况下master的儿子免试或减免费用，形成世袭壁垒
facts.source: Spanish guild history (maestro gremio)

facts.content: 黑死病后劳动力短缺导致工资上涨：1300-19年农业日工资3.85便士（小麦购买力基准100%），1360-79年涨至6.55便士（小麦购买力154%），1380-99年涨至7.22便士（小麦购买力235%）
facts.source: Wages and prices in medieval England, Winchester estates data

contradicts: F06（商人买市政官职很普遍）- 稿子里区分两种路径：普通大商人买地方官职爬社会阶梯（FS04）vs top银行家用国家债务leverage直接获得矿产垄断权和政治决策权（FS06-07），后者才是'creditor说了算但又不敢pull'的悖论级别

F07（Charles V 1522年财政极差Fugger威胁停贷）+ F20（Philip II破产Fugger巨亏）- 稿子里正面处理leverage的双刃剑：1522年leverage最大时Fugger确实能威胁停贷迫使还款（FS06），但到1557/1575 Philip II破产时Fugger已经借太多、不敢停贷、最终巨亏（FS08）。论点从'债主说了算'升级为'债主在debt restructuring那一刻说了算，但欠太多时反而被锁死'。
thesis_check.note: 论点用F01/F05/F02/F03撑住债权leverage的权力面，用F10/F20撑住leverage的风险面（债主也会破产）。F06和F07不推翻论点而是丰富它：F06区分地方买官vs国家债务两种scale，F07+F20展示leverage从有效（1522威胁停贷）到失效（1557欠太多不敢停）的转折。结尾必须同时落'creditor那一栏'和'不敢pull the plug'两面，才和事实一致。

modules.retention_role: identity_entry：12岁学徒身份标签、行会规则揭示、官员贿赂的第一次可见、一次失误的绝对后果
modules.reason: 你12岁，手上沾着靛蓝染料（F12: 学徒12-14岁开始）。师傅教你怎么认行会印章——只有印章对的货才能在市场卖，错的会被city watch没收、罚款（F08: 行会禁止非成员交易）。你看到一个商人在city gate给官员塞钱，官员看都不看他的货就放行。师傅低声说：'记住这个，以后你也要学。'第二天你跟师傅去市场，一个没交保护费的小贩被抓、货物当街砸烂，city watch说'行会规矩'。你问师傅为什么不帮他，师傅说：'一次站错队，七年学徒白干。'（F11: 学徒期7年）这是你进入的第一天：规则、贿赂、一次失误的代价。

modules.retention_role: evidence_build：持有PK01（commenda不对等分成）和PK02（父亲海难丧生）
modules.reason: 七年后你19岁，终于可以离开师傅的作坊。一个威尼斯商人找到你：他出300 ducats买一船布料，你负责运到热那亚卖掉，利润你拿1/4、他拿3/4（F19: unilateral commenda分成）。你问为什么他拿更多，他说：'因为船沉了是我的钱没了，你只是白跑一趟。'（F15/F19: 出资者承担全部财产风险）你想起父亲——他也是这样一个旅行商人，五年前在去比萨的路上遇到风暴，船和货一起沉了，家里什么都没拿回来（PK02: 家庭创伤 dark_reveal 75）。出资的商人只是换了个合伙人继续做，你妈妈却守寡到现在。你接下这单，因为1/4的利润是75 ducats——你七年学徒一分钱工资都没拿过（F12: 学徒无工资），这是你人生第一笔钱。

modules.retention_role: conflict_escalation：持有PK03（行会垄断导致物价上涨、官员忽视抱怨）
modules.reason: 你30岁，刚成为行会master（F14: 成为master需60天工资入会费，约15周收入）。行会给你的第一个权力是：城里所有卖布料的人必须从你们这13个master手里进货，直接从外地进货的会被city watch没收、罚到破产（F08: 行会垄断）。你和其他master商量好：布料统一涨价20%。市场上开始有抱怨——裁缝说布贵了、做一件衣服要多收客人3先令，客人说穿不起新衣服了。有人去city hall告状，city magistrate（市政官）听完说'这是行会内部事务，我不管'然后就打发走了（PK03: 权力合谋 dark_reveal 80）。你后来知道：那个magistrate每年从行会收2,000先令'咨询费'（F06: 商人购买官职/贿赂官员）。物价涨了，平民抱怨了，官员装没听见。你的收入翻了一倍。

modules.retention_role: evidence_build：持有PK04（破产商人公开羞辱）
modules.reason: 你35岁，已经有三个apprentice、两个journeyman。有一天city square（市政广场）聚集了一大群人，你挤过去看：一个你认识的布商，两年前还和你一起喝酒，现在被绑在wooden platform（木台）上，city crier（城市传令官）大声念他的债务清单——欠12个creditor总共8,000 florins，跑了三个月被抓回来（F17: 破产商人被逮捕）。他的货物、作坊、甚至家里的家具都被当街拍卖，city watch站在旁边防止有人闹事。人群里有人喊'骗子''还钱'，有小孩朝他扔烂菜叶。拍卖结束，city crier宣布：所有财产卖了5,000 florins，还欠3,000，他会被关进debtors' prison（债务人监狱）直到家人凑够钱或者creditor同意放人（PK04: 公开羞辱 dark_reveal 75）。你看着他被押走，想起那天他请你喝酒时说的话：'再做一单大的，就能还清了。'

modules.retention_role: worldview_upgrade：持有PK05（银行家家庭牺牲）和PK06（因怀疑背叛切断资金）
modules.reason: 你45岁，不再自己跑生意了。你有12个agents分布在威尼斯、安特卫普、里昂，专门做一件事：借钱给duke（公爵）、prince（亲王）、有时候是king（F04: Fugger借钱给Ferdinand I/Charles V）。1537年奥地利大公Ferdinand找你借83,000 florins买军备，年息14%（F04）。你借了，因为你知道一个秘密：大公的哥哥Charles V欠另一个银行家Fugger已经超过1 million florins了（F04: 1539年Fugger对Charles V债权1.25M）。借给royalty（王室）的钱，利息高、风险也高，但如果成了你能拿到的不只是钱——是mines（矿山）、是trade monopoly（贸易垄断权）、是city magistrate的任命权。但代价也在累积：你女儿15岁时你在安特卫普谈一笔30万florins的loan，没能回去参加她的betrothal feast（订婚宴）；你母亲去世时你在威尼斯盯着一个duke的还款，连葬礼都没赶上（PK05: 家庭牺牲 emotional_payoff 85）。更危险的是信任：去年你的一个partner（合伙人），你借给他20,000 florins做威尼斯-伦敦航线，有人告诉你他在secretly negotiating（秘密谈判）把货转卖给你的competitor（竞争对手）。你没有证据，但你不能等——你cut off his credit line（切断他的信用额度），三个月后他破产了（PK06: 切断资金导致破产 dark_reveal 75）。后来你发现那是谣言，但已经晚了。在这个level（级别），怀疑就是verdict（判决）。

modules.retention_role: conflict_escalation：持有PK07（破产后的终极对照）
modules.reason: 你55岁。1557年，你一生中最大的debtor（债务人）——西班牙国王Philip II——宣布bankruptcy（破产）。他欠你的那部分debt：1,660,809 ducats（F20: Fugger在西班牙债权），外加他三年前'temporarily requisitioned'（临时征用）你的silver shipment（白银货运）、到现在还扣在royal treasury（皇家金库）里的762,262 crowns（F20）。你以为你能negotiate（谈判），因为1522年你的前辈Jakob Fugger威胁stop lending（停贷）、成功逼Charles V还了钱（F07: Fugger 1522威胁停贷）。但这次不一样：Philip II欠的钱已经太多了，多到如果你真的stop、他就彻底default（违约），那你这辈子借出去的2 million ducats就永远拿不回来了。所以你不敢stop，你只能继续借、继续等、继续祈祷他有一天能还一部分。1575年他第二次破产（F20: Philip II 1575二次破产），第二年安特卫普被sack（洗劫），你在那里的branch office（分行）被烧、account books（账本）全毁。你曾经给emperor（皇帝）写信说'没有我你不可能获得那顶王冠'（F05），现在你住在Augsburg的fortified house（防御庄园）里，不敢出门、不敢见creditor、不敢让家族其他成员知道亏了多少（PK07: 帝国与囚笼对照 dark_payoff 85）。你拥有过两座silver mines（F03: Fugger矿产垄断权），现在你拥有的是一堆never-to-be-repaid IOUs（永远收不回的欠条）和一个不敢离开的房子。

analysis.core_dilemma: 当国王欠你的钱已经到了he can't repay but you can't stop lending的临界点时，你是继续借（leverage更深但风险巨大，国王破产你全亏）还是停贷（保住已借出的本金但永远收不回来，且失去所有政治影响力）？Jakob Fugger 1522年成功威胁停贷逼Charles V还款（F07），但到1557年Philip II欠Fugger 1.66M ducats时Fugger不敢停、继续借、最终在1557/1575两次破产中巨亏（F20）。Dilemma的核心：你借得越多权力越大，但到某个点之后权力反转——不是你控制国王，而是国王的债务规模把你锁死了。

title.final_title: Every Level of a Medieval Merchant
title.viewer_question: 中世纪商人从最底层到最高层是什么样的？每一级做什么、赚多少、付出什么代价？最顶层的商人有多大权力？
title.expected_answer_direction: 期待看到从学徒到富商的完整路径，每一级的生活细节、收入增长、社会地位提升

protagonist.who: 中世纪欧洲的商人（从12岁学徒开始，经历apprentice→journeyman→master→merchant→banker的完整路径）
protagonist.era: 中世纪晚期到文艺复兴早期（约1300-1550）
protagonist.place: 欧洲商业城市（主要是意大利佛罗伦萨、德国奥格斯堡、英国伦敦、法国里昂等贸易中心）
protagonist.source_role: 原片主角是墨西哥卡特尔成员（男性），从最底层望风者到最高层头目
protagonist.mapping: 原片'组织'→本题'行会/商业网络'；原片'地盘'→本题'市场垄断/贸易路线'；原片'暴力'→本题'经济leverage/债权'；原片'警察'→本题'城市官员/国王'；称呼都是第二人称'你'不变

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 中世纪商人就是做买卖的生意人，靠卖货赚钱，和国王贵族是两个世界
thesis_card.truth: 顶级商人（Fugger/Medici级别）不再靠卖货，他们成为政权的债主：借钱给国王打仗、用债务换矿产垄断权和政治决策权，国王欠他们的钱比国库还多
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 中世纪商人的最高级不是卖得最多的人，而是让国王欠你钱、还不起时你说了算的人
thesis_card.ending_landing: 今天谁的presentation最重要？不是title最大的那个人，而是资产负债表creditor那一栏里写着名字的人。Peruzzi破产了，但下一个Medici已经在路上。街角永远有新的12岁学徒，手上沾着染料，不知道30年后他会决定哪个国王能保住王冠。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论是'暴力只是表层，真正支撑它的是政商网络；头目只是可替换零件，系统永续'。本题结论是'贸易只是表层，真正的权力是债权leverage；商人个体可以破产，但债权-政权共生关系永续'。核心逻辑相同（表层vs深层、个人vs系统永续），但内容从暴力犯罪换成金融政治。
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为中世纪商人靠卖货赚钱、和王权是两个世界，实际顶级商人用债务leverage控制政权，Charles V 1523年写信承认'没有Fugger不可能获得罗马皇冠'
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样是欠债不还：普通商人欠钱会被公开羞辱、财产没收、关进债务人监狱；国王欠Fugger 20 million ducats却能继续借、还能用矿产开采权抵债

contradicts: F06（商人买市政官职很普遍，不只是债权换来的）- 稿子里区分两种路径：普通商人买地方官职爬social ladder vs top银行家用债务leverage直接获得国家级垄断权，后者才是'股东'级别
F07（Charles V 1522年财政极差，Fugger威胁停贷）- 稿子里用这个说明风险：国王可以赖账，但在debt leverage最大的那几年商人确实hold power；对应到结尾'creditor不等于owner，但debt restructuring那一刻你说了算'
thesis_check.note: 论点用F01-F05撑住：Fugger 1519年借543k选举款、1523年写强硬信、1540s Charles V欠20M、用债务换矿产垄断权。F06和F07是相反的事实但不推翻论点：F06说明买官普遍但本片聚焦top-tier的债权leverage（不是普通买官）；F07说明债主地位有风险但在leverage最大时确实有power。这两条在稿中要正面处理，不能藏。

analysis_original.core_dilemma: 当国王欠你的钱已经还不起时，你是继续借（风险更大但leverage更深）还是停贷（保住已有资产但失去政治影响力）？Fugger 1522年威胁停贷迫使Charles V还款，但最终Fugger在Philip II破产时巨亏。

hook.contract: immediate_second_person_drop：第一个刺激0.2秒（你12岁，手上沾着染料），第一个甜头0.2秒（30年后你会决定哪个国王能保住王冠），开场窗口0-30秒

candidates.text: 你12岁。手上沾着靛蓝染料。30年后，你会写一封信，告诉神圣罗马帝国皇帝：没有我，你不可能戴上那顶王冠。
你12岁。师傅刚教你怎么看行会印章。30年后，国王会欠你543,000金弗罗林——比他国库里的钱还多。
你12岁。今天你第一次看到官员收贿赂。30年后，你会拥有两座银矿——不是买的，是国王用来抵债的。

hook.why: 第一个候选用F05（Jakob Fugger 1523年的强硬信件）做甜头，最能体现论点'债主说了算'，而且'写一封信告诉皇帝'比单纯的数字更有画面感和power dynamics。第一个甜头5秒落地，符合开场契约。

risks: 关键数据缺口：7个'待查'事实（F10-F17, F19）中，F10（Peruzzi破产）、F15（旅行风险）、F17（破产下场）直接影响3个高峰（PK02, PK04, PK07），必须补齐才能写稿
论点边界窄：只适用于top-tier银行家（Fugger/Medici），不适用于普通商人，需要在开头或中段明确说明'这不是所有商人的故事'
时代跨度大：从学徒到银行家需要30-40年，如果严格按'同一个人'的POV写，年龄跨度从12岁到50岁，中间需要有时间流逝的标记
国王赖账风险：F07说明债主地位不稳定（Charles V 1522年财政差、Fugger威胁停贷），必须在稿中正面处理，不能只讲leverage不讲风险
双重标准（F06）：普通商人买地方官职vs银行家用债务leverage国家政策，两者scale差异需要在FS04或FS06明确区分，否则观众会觉得'买官很普遍，没什么特别的'
无真人案例：cases字段为空，缺少具体的店主或个人故事，全片只有Fugger/Medici这种大家族，可能显得抽象。建议补充1-2个小商人或journeyman的具体案例作为对比

analysis_before_adjust.verdict_reason: 框架核心机制（层级沉浸叙事、职责-收入-代价三件套、暴力到政商的浓度渐变、循环结尾）在中世纪商人题材中都能实现。需要7个换内容保功能的调整：把原片的暴力犯罪机制（警察收买、货物伪装、地盘战争、平民伤亡、恐怖展示、处决手下）换成商业金融机制（官员贿赂、货物运输风险、行会垄断、物价上涨、破产羞辱、切断资金）来承担同样的留存高峰。所有调整都是普通段的内容替换，锁定项（开场钩子、悬念开合、循环结尾）可以做到。

title.final_title: Every Level of a Medieval Merchant
title.viewer_question: 中世纪商人从最底层到最高层是什么样的？每一级做什么、赚多少、付出什么代价？最顶层的商人有多大权力？
title.expected_answer_direction: 期待看到从学徒到富商的完整路径，每一级的生活细节、收入增长、社会地位提升

protagonist.who: 中世纪欧洲的商人（从12岁学徒开始，经历apprentice→journeyman→master→merchant→banker的完整路径）
protagonist.era: 中世纪晚期到文艺复兴早期（约1300-1550）
protagonist.place: 欧洲商业城市（主要是意大利佛罗伦萨、德国奥格斯堡、英国伦敦、法国里昂等贸易中心）
protagonist.source_role: 原片主角是墨西哥卡特尔成员（男性），从最底层望风者到最高层头目
protagonist.mapping: 原片'组织'→本题'行会/商业网络'；原片'地盘'→本题'市场垄断/贸易路线'；原片'暴力'→本题'经济leverage/债权'；原片'警察'→本题'城市官员/国王'；称呼都是第二人称'你'不变

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 中世纪商人就是做买卖的生意人，靠卖货赚钱，和国王贵族是两个世界
thesis_card.truth: 顶级商人（Fugger/Medici级别）不再靠卖货，他们成为政权的债主：借钱给国王打仗、用债务换矿产垄断权和政治决策权，国王欠他们的钱比国库还多
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 中世纪商人的最高级不是卖得最多的人，而是让国王欠你钱、还不起时你说了算的人
thesis_card.ending_landing: 今天谁的presentation最重要？不是title最大的那个人，而是资产负债表creditor那一栏里写着名字的人。Peruzzi破产了，但下一个Medici已经在路上。街角永远有新的12岁学徒，手上沾着染料，不知道30年后他会决定哪个国王能保住王冠。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论是'暴力只是表层，真正支撑它的是政商网络；头目只是可替换零件，系统永续'。本题结论是'贸易只是表层，真正的权力是债权leverage；商人个体可以破产，但债权-政权共生关系永续'。核心逻辑相同（表层vs深层、个人vs系统永续），但内容从暴力犯罪换成金融政治。
thesis_card.contrast: 翻案：观众以为中世纪商人靠卖货赚钱、和王权是两个世界，实际顶级商人用债务leverage控制政权，Charles V 1523年写信承认'没有Fugger不可能获得罗马皇冠'
thesis_card.double_standard: 同样是欠债不还：普通商人欠钱会被公开羞辱、财产没收、关进债务人监狱；国王欠Fugger 20 million ducats却能继续借、还能用矿产开采权抵债
thesis_card.boundary: 论点只适用于top-tier银行家族（Fugger/Medici/Peruzzi级别），不适用于地方行会商人或普通行脚贸易商；时间主要是15-16世纪欧洲王权财政危机期

rows.function: 权力彻底反转，最大债务人宣布破产，债主的leverage瞬间失效，从能威胁国王到不敢停贷的锁死状态
rows.keep: 观众看到国王破产的具体时刻，债主手里的巨额债权变成废纸，曾经的leverage变成无法脱身的陷阱
rows.swap: 换成Philip II 1557破产公告、Fugger的具体损失数字、被扣押的银矿银子、债主从leverage最大到被锁死的转折
rows.reason: 这是核心反转段，必须用新题目自己的破产事实，不能照搬原片的反转逻辑

rows.function: 系统循环确认，前一代债主破产后下一代已在崛起，街角永远有新学徒，回扣开头的底层起点
rows.keep: 观众看到破产不是终点而是循环的一部分，新的银行家家族已在路上，新的学徒又开始同样的路径
rows.swap: 换成Peruzzi破产后Medici崛起的历史循环、新学徒的年龄和起点、结尾落点改为creditor那一栏里的名字
rows.reason: 结尾回扣和最后一个高峰必须保留，用Peruzzi-Medici循环完成系统永续性的确认

reversal.new_reversal: 观众以为债主leverage在债务最大时说了算，真相是欠太多时债主反而被锁死——停贷国王就破产、债权全废，不停贷就继续亏，1557年Philip II破产Fugger损失166万ducats加被扣押银矿

ladder.why: 原片有 4 段是同一种功能(conflict_escalation:FS03、FS04、FS07、FS08);写前分析判的叙事方式是「同一个人往上爬」

[CH01 | 0:00-1:10 | 底层学徒通过具体场景第一次接触行会规则和官员腐败，理解违规的绝对后果]

You're twelve years old. Your hands are stained indigo blue. Thirty years from now, you'll write a letter to the Holy Roman Emperor: without me, you never could have worn that crown.

But today you don't own anything. Not even the clothes on your back.

You became an apprentice this morning. Your master is a wool merchant. You live in his house now. You eat at his table. You sleep in the room above his workshop. For the next seven years, you won't receive a single coin.

Your master shows you a wax seal. The guild mark. He presses it into red wax on a bolt of cloth. "Only this mark," he says. "Goods without it get seized at the market. The city watch confiscates everything. They fine you more than the cloth is worth."

You watch him wrap the bolt. He hands you a bundle to carry.

At the city gate, a merchant ahead of you slips coins into the guard's hand. The guard doesn't check his cart. Doesn't ask for papers. Just waves him through.

Your master leans close. "Remember this. You'll need to learn it later."

The next morning at the market square, you see a man selling leather without the guild seal. Two members of the city watch grab his goods. They smash his leather pouches on the cobblestones. The crowd watches. No one helps.

The watch captain announces: "Guild regulations. Non-members cannot trade within city walls."

You ask your master why no one stopped them.

He says: "Stand with the wrong side once, and your seven years count for nothing. You'll never become a master. You'll stay an apprentice until you're too old to matter."

That's the first lesson. There are rules. There are people who enforce them. There are people who pay not to follow them.

And there's a line you can't cross.

[CH02 | 1:10-2:44 | 新人承接第一个高风险任务，通过commenda合伙看到不对等的风险分配，目睹家庭成员可被替换的残酷]

Seven years pass. You're nineteen.

A Venetian merchant finds you. He needs someone to travel.

He puts 300 ducats on the table. That's the capital. He's buying cloth in Venice. You sail it to Genoa and sell it.

The profit splits this way: three-quarters to him, one-quarter to you.

You ask why he takes more.

He says: "Because if the ship sinks, it's my money at the bottom of the sea. You just wasted a trip."

That's the commenda. The investor stays on land. He risks his capital. You risk your body.

If pirates take the ship, he loses 300 ducats. You lose your life.

If a storm hits and the cargo's ruined, he's out the investment. You're out nothing — except the months you spent at sea for no pay.

You think of your father.

He was a traveling merchant too. Five years ago, he took a commenda contract to Pisa. The ship ran into a storm off Livorno. The cargo sank. He drowned with it.

The investor? He found a new partner the next month. Same terms. Same split. Just a different body on the ship.

Your mother got nothing. No compensation. No final payment. The investor didn't even attend the funeral.

She's been a widow ever since. You've been fatherless.

But you take the contract.

Because one-quarter of the profit is 75 ducats. And in seven years as an apprentice, you never earned a single coin. Your master gave you food, a place to sleep, and training. No wages.

This is your first money.

You ask yourself: how many trips like this until you can afford to be the one who stays on land? How long until you're the investor, not the body on the ship?

[CH03 | 2:44-4:10 | 身份升级后收入明显增长，生活条件改善，但同时暴露在更高层级的威胁中]

Six years. You make that trip fourteen times. You survive storms, pirates, cargo losses. You bank your quarter-shares.

Now you're 25. A journeyman. You don't need a master's roof anymore.

The work changed. No more months at sea. You hire out your skills by the day. Carpentry, most weeks. Three pence a day for standard work. Four if you're fast. Five in London when they're desperate.

You run the numbers. Three pence buys two loaves and a room for the night. Before the plague killed half the workers, three pence bought you just the bread. Now it buys more. The masters complain. You don't.

You rent a room above a tavern. Your own door. Your own lock. You eat meat twice a week. You buy a second shirt.

But the room comes with a neighbor. Another journeyman. He works for a Flemish merchant who pays six pence a day and doesn't care about guild rules. The Flemish merchant brings in goods from Antwerp, undercuts local prices, takes contracts the guild says belong to local masters.

Your masters notice. They ask questions. Who's working for outsiders? Who's breaking rates?

You keep your head down. The Flemish merchant's journeyman makes more. But he also knows: one complaint to the guild, and the city watch shuts him down. Confiscates the goods. Maybe worse.

You're making more than your father ever did. But now you're visible.

You start asking: how much does it cost to become a master? How long until you're the one setting the rates, not taking them?

[CH04 | 4:10-5:51 | 成为垄断链条中的一环，获得定价权但导致平民受损，权力方对伤亡虚无化]

You're 30. You're a guild master now.

It took five years. Every florin from those Genoa runs. You borrowed the rest. The entry fee: 60 days wages. Fifteen weeks of income. You paid.

The guild gives you a seal. Your mark on cloth means it can be sold in this city. Without it, the city watch confiscates. Fines the seller. Sometimes worse.

There are 13 masters in the cloth guild. That's it. Every tailor, every household, every merchant buying fabric — they buy from one of you thirteen. Not from outsiders. Not from journeymen working alone.

The guild calls a meeting. You sit with the other twelve. Someone says: prices should go up. Everyone nods. You vote. Unanimous.

Cloth prices rise 20% the next week.

At the market, you hear the complaints. A tailor says fabric costs more now. He has to charge customers three shillings extra per garment. Customers say they can't afford new clothes. They're making do with old ones.

Someone goes to city hall. Files a complaint. Says the guild is gouging the city.

The city magistrate listens. Then says: this is guild internal business. I don't manage that. He sends them away.

You learn why later. That magistrate takes 2,000 shillings a year from the guild. Consulting fee, they call it.

Prices went up. Commoners complained. The official heard nothing.

Your income doubled.

You think about the masterpiece exam you passed. The carved loom shuttle you made to prove your skill. Your father could never have done it. His father couldn't either. But their sons — if they're masters' sons — they skip the exam. Or pay less.

You earned this. That's what you tell yourself.

The system works. For you.

But you also know: this power exists because the magistrate looks away. Because the city watch enforces your monopoly, not the law.

How long does that last? What happens if someone stops looking away?

[CH05 | 5:51-7:48 | 目睹同级别人物因债务崩溃的完整过程，理解信用体系的死亡线和破产的社会性死亡]

You're 35. Three apprentices. Two journeymen. Your workshop makes decent profit.

One morning you hear noise in the city square. You walk over.

A wooden platform in the center. A man tied to it. You recognize him.

Thomas. Cloth merchant. You drank with him two years ago. He paid for the wine.

Now a city crier stands beside him reading from a parchment. Loud enough for the crowd.

"Thomas Alderton. Debts to twelve creditors. Total: 8,000 florins."

The crier lists each one. Names. Amounts. When the debt was made.

"Fled three months ago. Captured in Bristol."

Thomas doesn't look up. His face is bruised.

Behind the platform: his inventory. Bales of wool. Bolts of linen. Tools. Furniture from his house.

The auction starts. City watch stands at each corner. No one moves.

People bid. Low. A competitor buys his best loom for half what it's worth.

The crowd isn't quiet. Someone yells "thief." Someone throws a turnip. It hits his shoulder.

A child near you asks his mother who the man is. She says "someone who didn't pay."

The auction ends. Total collected: 5,000 florins.

The crier announces: "Still owed: 3,000 florins. The debtor will be held in prison until family or creditors settle the balance."

Three thousand florins. That's what stands between Thomas and freedom.

In Bruges, the records show, a merchant named Veckinchusen was held for three years. Three years in a debtors' cell waiting for someone to pay.

Some cities are worse. Florence's law says it plainly: bankrupt merchants are permanently exiled. Eiectio a civitate. Driven from the city. Citizenship stripped. Your children inherit the ban.

You watch them untie Thomas. Lead him away.

The crowd disperses. Someone picks up the turnip.

You walk back to your workshop. Your apprentice asks where you went. You don't answer.

That night you count your own debts. The loan you took to expand the workshop. The advance you gave a supplier who hasn't delivered. The guild fees due next month.

You're not at 8,000. Not yet. But you're not at zero either.

Thomas paid for wine two years ago. Now he's in a cell with no window.

The distance between those two moments: one bad shipment. One customer who doesn't pay. One creditor who stops waiting.

You lock the strongbox. Check it twice.

There has to be a way to avoid this. A level where debt doesn't destroy you.

A level where you're the one holding the ledger, not tied to the platform.

What does that level look like?

[CH06 | 7:48-9:53 | 身份彻底改变成为借钱给统治者的债主，债务规模和抵押物等级跃升，但信任瓦解和家庭牺牲]

You're 45. You don't run the goods yourself anymore.

You have 12 agents. Venice. Antwerp. Lyon. Augsburg. Each one does the same thing: lend money to dukes, to princes, sometimes to kings.

1537. Archduke Ferdinand needs 83,000 florins for military supplies. 14% annual interest. You lend it. You know a secret: his brother Charles V already owes another banker over a million florins.

When you lend to royalty, you don't get just interest. You get mines. Trade monopolies. The right to name city magistrates.

But the cost accumulates in a different ledger.

Your daughter turns 15. You're in Antwerp negotiating a 300,000 florin loan. You miss her betrothal feast. She writes you a letter. You read it three months later.

Your mother dies. You're in Venice watching a duke's repayment. You don't make it to the funeral.

The agents send reports. You read them in a room with locked doors. The numbers grow. The distances grow.

Last year, one of your partners. You lent him 20,000 florins for the Venice-London route. Someone tells you he's secretly negotiating to sell the cargo to your competitor.

You have no proof. But you can't wait.

You cut his credit line.

Three months later, he's bankrupt. His warehouse auctioned in the square. His family leaves the city.

Then you find out: it was a rumor. The informant misheard a conversation at an inn.

But it's too late. The credit is gone. The business is gone. The man is gone.

You write a letter to his widow. You don't send it.

At this level, suspicion is verdict.

You can't trust partners. You can't trust agents. The numbers in the ledgers are too large. One betrayal, one miscalculation, and you're the one tied to the platform.

You have mines in Spain. Silver from Guadalcanal. Mercury from Almadén. Collateral from kings.

You have everything a merchant could want.

Your daughter doesn't recognize your handwriting anymore. Your mother's grave has your brother's name on the stone, not yours.

You sit in a fortified house. The reports come every week. Ferdinand owes you 83,000. Charles owes you more. Much more.

You wonder: how much can one king owe? How much leverage is too much?

What happens when the numbers get so large that you're not the one holding the ledger anymore—you're the one locked inside it?

[CH07 | 9:53-11:26 | 展示债权帝国的量化规模，债主与国王的leverage在巅峰时刻的具体表现]

You're 50 years old.

The numbers are now so large they stop feeling like money.

Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, owes creditors across Europe close to 20 million ducats. Your family holds a major portion of that debt.

In 1539, just his debts to you: 1.25 million florins. That's more than the annual revenue of most kingdoms.

But here's what leverage really looks like.

1522. Charles's credit is so bad no one will lend. His treasury is empty. He needs funds to hold his empire together.

You write him a letter. April 24, 1523.

"It is well known that Your Imperial Majesty could not have acquired the Roman crown without my help."

You're not asking. You're stating a fact. Then you make it clear: pay what you owe, or I stop lending.

He pays.

That's leverage at its peak. You can make an emperor bend.

But here's what you also know, sitting in that fortified house reading the weekly reports:

The debt is so large now that if he couldn't pay, you'd lose everything. You've lent so much that his collapse would be your collapse.

The same leverage that lets you threaten him also chains you to him.

Leverage works—until the debtor owes more than he can ever repay. Then you can't pull the rope without hanging yourself.

Will this leverage hold? Will the king keep paying?

Or is there a point where the debt gets so large that threatening to stop becomes a threat to yourself?

[CH08 | 11:26-12:13 | 权力彻底反转，最大债务人破产，债主的leverage瞬间失效，从能威胁国王到被锁死的状态]

You're 55 years old.

1557. Philip II declares bankruptcy. He owes you 1,660,809 ducats. Plus 762,262 crowns in silver he "temporarily requisitioned" three years ago—still sitting in his treasury.

You think you can negotiate. In 1522, Jakob Fugger threatened to stop lending. Charles V paid.

But this time is different. Philip owes too much. If you actually stop, he defaults completely. Then your 2 million ducats in loans—gone forever.

So you can't stop. You keep lending. Keep waiting. Keep praying he'll repay something.

1575. He bankrupts again. 1576, Antwerp is sacked. Your branch office burns. Account books destroyed.

You once wrote to an emperor: "Without me, you could not have obtained that crown."

Now you live in a fortified house in Augsburg. You can't leave. Can't face creditors. Can't let family know how much you've lost.

You own two silver mines. What you actually own: a stack of never-to-be-repaid IOUs and a house you're afraid to leave.

But will your empire die with you? Who takes over next?

[CH09 | 12:13-13:00 | 系统循环确认，前一代债主破产后下一代已在崛起，街角永远有新学徒，回扣开头]

The system doesn't stop with you.

Fourteen years earlier, Edward III defaulted. Peruzzi and Bardi collapsed. Total loss: 1,365,000 florins.

Fifty years later, a new house opened in Florence. The Medici. 1397.

They learned from Peruzzi's mistakes. They made the same ones anyway.

Right now, somewhere in Augsburg, there's a boy. Twelve years old. Hands stained with indigo dye.

He doesn't know that in thirty years, he'll write a letter to an emperor: "Without me, you could not have obtained that crown."

He doesn't know that ten years after that, the king will owe him so much he can't ask for it back.

Next time you see a balance sheet, look at the creditor column.

The most important name isn't the one with the biggest title.

It's the one who's owed too much to walk away.

# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-1:10 | 底层学徒通过具体场景第一次接触行会规则和官员腐败，理解违规的绝对后果]

Every merchant starts at level one. Apprentice. That's you.

You're twelve years old. Your hands are stained indigo blue. Thirty years from now, you'll write a letter to the Holy Roman Emperor: without me, you never could have worn that crown.

But today you don't own anything. Not even the clothes on your back.

You became an apprentice this morning. Your master is a wool merchant. You live in his house now. You eat at his table. You sleep in the room above his workshop. For the next seven years, you won't receive a single coin.

Your master shows you a wax seal. The guild mark. He presses it into red wax on a bolt of cloth. "Only this mark," he says. "Goods without it get seized at the market. The city watch confiscates everything. They fine you more than the cloth is worth."

At the city gate, a merchant ahead of you slips coins into the guard's hand. The guard doesn't check his cart. Doesn't ask for papers. Just waves him through.

Your master leans close. "Remember this. You'll need to learn it later."

The next morning at the market square, you see a man selling leather without the guild seal. Two members of the city watch grab his goods. They smash his leather pouches on the cobblestones. The crowd watches. No one helps.

The watch captain announces: "Guild regulations. Non-members cannot trade within city walls."

You ask your master why no one stopped them.

He says: "Stand with the wrong side once, and your seven years count for nothing. You'll never become a master. You'll stay an apprentice until you're too old to matter."

That's the first lesson. There are rules. There are people who enforce them. There are people who pay not to follow them.

And there's a line you can't cross.

[CH02 | 1:10-2:44 | 新人承接第一个高风险任务，通过commenda合伙看到不对等的风险分配，目睹家庭成员可被替换的残酷]

Seven years pass. You're nineteen.

A Venetian merchant finds you. He needs someone to travel.

He puts 300 ducats on the table. That's the capital. He's buying cloth in Venice. You sail it to Genoa and sell it.

The profit splits this way: three-quarters to him, one-quarter to you.

You ask why he takes more.

He says: "Because if the ship sinks, it's my money at the bottom of the sea. You just wasted a trip."

That's the commenda. The investor stays on land. He risks his capital. You risk your body.

If pirates take the ship, he loses 300 ducats. You lose your life.

If a storm hits and the cargo's ruined, he's out the investment. You're out nothing — except the months you spent at sea for no pay.

You think of your father.

He was a traveling merchant too. Five years ago, he took a commenda contract to Pisa. The ship ran into a storm off Livorno. The cargo sank. He drowned with it.

The investor? He found a new partner the next month. Same terms. Same split. Just a different body on the ship.

Your mother got nothing. No compensation. No final payment. The investor didn't even attend the funeral.

She's been a widow ever since. You've been fatherless.

But you take the contract.

Because one-quarter of the profit is 75 ducats. And in seven years as an apprentice, you never earned a single coin. Your master gave you food, a place to sleep, and training. No wages.

This is your first money.

You ask yourself: how many trips like this until you can afford to be the one who stays on land? How long until you're the investor, not the body on the ship?

[CH03 | 2:44-4:10 | 身份升级后收入明显增长，生活条件改善，但同时暴露在更高层级的威胁中]

Six years. You make that trip fourteen times. You survive storms, pirates, cargo losses. You bank your quarter-shares.

Now you're 25. A journeyman. You don't need a master's roof anymore.

The work changed. No more months at sea. You hire out your skills by the day. Carpentry, most weeks. Three pence a day for standard work. Four if you're fast. Five in London when they're desperate.

Three pence buys two loaves and a room for the night. Before the plague killed half the workers, three pence bought you just the bread. Now it buys more. The masters complain. You don't.

You rent a room above a tavern. Your own door. Your own lock. You eat meat twice a week. You buy a second shirt.

But the room comes with a neighbor. Another journeyman. He works for a Flemish merchant who pays six pence a day and doesn't care about guild rules. The Flemish merchant brings in goods from Antwerp, undercuts local prices, takes contracts the guild says belong to local masters.

Your masters notice. They ask questions. Who's working for outsiders? Who's breaking rates?

You keep your head down. The Flemish merchant's journeyman makes more. But he also knows: one complaint to the guild, and the city watch shuts him down. Confiscates the goods. Maybe worse.

You're making more than your father ever did. But now you're visible.

You start asking: how much does it cost to become a master? How long until you're the one setting the rates, not taking them?

[CH04 | 4:10-5:51 | 成为垄断链条中的一环，获得定价权但导致平民受损，权力方对伤亡虚无化]

You're 30. You're a guild master now.

It took five years. Every florin from those Genoa runs. You borrowed the rest. The entry fee: fifteen weeks of income. You paid.

The guild gives you a seal. Your mark on cloth means it can be sold in this city. Without it, the city watch confiscates. Fines the seller. Sometimes worse.

The guild calls a meeting. You sit with the other masters. Someone says: prices should go up. Everyone nods. You vote. Unanimous.

Cloth prices rise the next week.

At the market, you hear the complaints. A tailor says fabric costs more now. He has to charge customers extra per garment. Customers say they can't afford new clothes. They're making do with old ones.

Someone goes to city hall. Files a complaint. Says the guild is gouging the city.

The city magistrate listens. Then says: this is guild internal business. I don't manage that. He sends them away.

You learn why later. That magistrate was a guild master himself before taking office.

Prices went up. Commoners complained. The official heard nothing.

Your income doubled.

You think about the masterpiece exam you passed. The carved loom shuttle you made to prove your skill. Your father could never have done it. His father couldn't either. But their sons — if they're masters' sons — they skip the exam. Or pay less.

You earned this. That's what you tell yourself.

The system works. For you.

But you also know: this power exists because the magistrate looks away. Because the city watch enforces your monopoly, not the law.

How long does that last? What happens if someone stops looking away?

[CH05 | 5:51-7:48 | 目睹同级别人物因债务崩溃的完整过程，理解信用体系的死亡线和破产的社会性死亡]

You're 35. Three apprentices. Two journeymen. Your workshop makes decent profit.

One morning you hear noise in the city square. You walk over.

A wooden platform in the center. A man tied to it. You recognize him.

You drank with him two years ago. He paid for the wine.

Now a city crier stands beside him reading from a parchment. Loud enough for the crowd.

The crier lists debts. Names. Amounts. When each debt was made.

"Fled three months ago. Captured in Bristol."

He doesn't look up. His face is bruised.

Behind the platform: his inventory. Bales of wool. Bolts of linen. Tools. Furniture from his house.

The auction starts. City watch stands at each corner. No one moves.

People bid. Low. A competitor buys his best loom for half what it's worth.

The crowd isn't quiet. Someone yells "thief." Someone throws a turnip. It hits his shoulder.

A child near you asks his mother who the man is. She says "someone who didn't pay."

The auction ends.

The crier announces: "The debtor will be held in prison until family or creditors settle the balance."

You watch them untie him. Lead him away.

The crowd disperses. Someone picks up the turnip.

You walk back to your workshop. Your apprentice asks where you went. You don't answer.

That night you count your own debts. The loan you took to expand the workshop. The advance you gave a supplier who hasn't delivered. The guild fees due next month.

The records show a merchant named Veckinchusen was held for three years. Three years in a debtors' cell waiting for someone to pay.

In Florence, the law says it plainly: bankrupt merchants are permanently exiled. Driven from the city. Citizenship stripped. Your children inherit the ban.

He paid for wine two years ago. Now he's in a cell with no window.

The distance between those two moments: one bad shipment. One customer who doesn't pay. One creditor who stops waiting.

You lock the strongbox. Check it twice.

There has to be a way to avoid this. A level where debt doesn't destroy you.

A level where you're the one holding the ledger, not tied to the platform.

What does that level look like?

[CH06 | 7:48-9:53 | 身份彻底改变成为借钱给统治者的债主，债务规模和抵押物等级跃升，但信任瓦解和家庭牺牲]

You're 45. You don't run the goods yourself anymore.

You have twelve agents. Venice. Antwerp. Lyon. Augsburg. Each one does the same thing: lend money to dukes, to princes, sometimes to kings.

1537. Archduke Ferdinand needs 83,000 florins for military supplies. Fourteen percent annual interest. You lend it.

When you lend to royalty, you don't get just interest. You get mines. Trade monopolies. The right to name city magistrates.

But the cost accumulates in a different ledger.

Your daughter turns 15. You're in Antwerp negotiating a 300,000 florin loan. You miss her betrothal feast. She writes you a letter. You read it three months later.

Your mother dies. You're in Venice watching a duke's repayment. You don't make it to the funeral.

The agents send reports. You read them in a room with locked doors. The numbers grow. The distances grow.

At this level, suspicion is verdict.

You can't trust partners. You can't trust agents. The numbers in the ledgers are too large. One betrayal, one miscalculation, and you're the one tied to the platform.

You have mines in Spain. Silver from Guadalcanal. Mercury from Almadén. Collateral from kings.

You have everything you could want. You have nothing you actually need.

Your daughter doesn't recognize your handwriting anymore. Your mother's grave has your brother's name on the stone, not yours.

You sit in a fortified house. The reports come every week. Ferdinand owes you 83,000. Charles owes you more. Much more.

You wonder: how much can one king owe? How much leverage is too much?

What happens when the numbers get so large that you're not the one holding the ledger anymore—you're the one locked inside it?

[CH07 | 9:53-11:26 | 展示债权帝国的量化规模，债主与国王的leverage在巅峰时刻的具体表现]

You're 42 years old.

The numbers are now so large they stop feeling like money.

Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, owes creditors across Europe close to 20 million ducats. Your family holds a major portion of that debt.

Just his debts to you: 1.25 million florins.

But here's what leverage really looks like.

1522. Charles's credit is so bad no one will lend. His treasury is empty. He needs funds to hold his empire together.

You write him a letter. April 24, 1523.

"It is well known that Your Imperial Majesty could not have acquired the Roman crown without my help."

You're not asking. You're stating a fact. Then you make it clear: pay what you owe, or I stop lending.

He pays.

That's leverage at its peak. You can make an emperor bend.

But here's what you also know, sitting in that fortified house reading the weekly reports:

The debt is so large now that if he couldn't pay, you'd lose everything. You've lent so much that his collapse would be your collapse.

The same leverage that lets you threaten him also chains you to him.

Leverage works—until the debtor owes more than he can ever repay. Then you can't pull the rope without hanging yourself.

Will this leverage hold? Will the king keep paying?

Or is there a point where the debt gets so large that threatening to stop becomes a threat to yourself?

[CH08 | 11:26-12:13 | 权力彻底反转，最大债务人破产，债主的leverage瞬间失效，从能威胁国王到被锁死的状态]

You're 55 years old.

1557. Philip II declares bankruptcy. He owes you 1,660,809 ducats. Plus 762,262 crowns in silver he "temporarily requisitioned" three years ago—still sitting in his treasury.

In 1522, your predecessor threatened to stop lending. Charles V paid.

But this time is different. Philip owes too much. If you actually stop, he defaults completely. Then your loans—gone forever.

So you can't stop. You keep lending. Keep waiting. Keep praying he'll repay something.

1575. He bankrupts again. 1576, Antwerp is sacked. Your branch office burns. Account books destroyed.

You once wrote to an emperor: "Without me, you could not have obtained that crown."

Now you live in a fortified house in Augsburg. You can't leave. Can't face creditors. Can't let family know how much you've lost.

You own two silver mines. What you actually own: a stack of never-to-be-repaid IOUs and a house you're afraid to leave.

But will your empire die with you? Who takes over next?

[CH09 | 12:13-13:00 | 系统循环确认，前一代债主破产后下一代已在崛起，街角永远有新学徒，回扣开头]

The system doesn't stop with you.

Sixty years earlier, Edward III defaulted. Peruzzi and Bardi collapsed. Total loss: 1,365,000 florins.

Fifty years later, a new house opened in Florence. The Medici. 1397.

They learned from Peruzzi's mistakes. They made the same ones anyway.

Right now, somewhere in Augsburg, there's a boy. Twelve years old. Hands stained with indigo dye.

He doesn't know that in thirty years, he'll write a letter to an emperor: "Without me, you could not have obtained that crown."

He doesn't know that thirteen years after that, the king will owe him so much he can't ask for it back.

Next time you see a balance sheet, look at the creditor column.

The most important name isn't the one with the biggest title.

It's the one who's owed too much to walk away.

[CH01 | 0:00-1:10 | 底层学徒通过具体场景第一次接触行会规则和官员腐败，理解违规的绝对后果]

Every merchant starts at level one. Apprentice. That's you.

You're twelve years old. Your hands are stained indigo blue. Thirty years from now, you'll write a letter to the Holy Roman Emperor: without me, you never could have worn that crown.

But today you don't own anything. Not even the clothes on your back.

You became an apprentice this morning. Your master is a wool merchant. You live in his house now. You eat at his table. You sleep in the room above his workshop. For the next seven years, you won't receive a single coin.

Your master shows you a wax seal. The guild mark. He presses it into red wax on a bolt of cloth. "Only this mark," he says. "Goods without it get seized at the market. The city watch confiscates everything. They fine you more than the cloth is worth."

At the city gate, a merchant ahead of you slips coins into the guard's hand. The guard doesn't check his cart. Doesn't ask for papers. Just waves him through.

Your master leans close. "Remember this. You'll need to learn it later."

The next morning at the market square, you see a man selling leather without the guild seal. Two members of the city watch grab his goods. They smash his leather pouches on the cobblestones. The crowd watches. No one helps.

The watch captain announces: "Guild regulations. Non-members cannot trade within city walls."

You ask your master why no one stopped them.

He says: "Stand with the wrong side once, and your seven years count for nothing. You'll never become a master. You'll stay an apprentice until you're too old to matter."

That's the first lesson. There are rules. There are people who enforce them. There are people who pay not to follow them.

And there's a line you can't cross.

[CH02 | 1:10-2:44 | 新人承接第一个高风险任务，通过commenda合伙看到不对等的风险分配，目睹家庭成员可被替换的残酷]

Seven years pass. You're nineteen.

A Venetian merchant finds you. He needs someone to travel.

He puts 300 ducats on the table. That's the capital. He's buying cloth in Venice. You sail it to Genoa and sell it.

The profit splits this way: three-quarters to him, one-quarter to you.

You ask why he takes more.

He says: "Because if the ship sinks, it's my money at the bottom of the sea. You just wasted a trip."

That's the commenda. The investor stays on land. He risks his capital. You risk your body.

If pirates take the ship, he loses 300 ducats. You lose your life.

If a storm hits and the cargo's ruined, he's out the investment. You're out nothing — except the months you spent at sea for no pay.

You think of your father.

He was a traveling merchant too. Five years ago, he took a commenda contract to Pisa. The ship ran into a storm off Livorno. The cargo sank. He drowned with it.

The investor? He found a new partner the next month. Same terms. Same split. Just a different body on the ship.

Your mother got nothing. No compensation. No final payment. The investor didn't even attend the funeral.

She's been a widow ever since. You've been fatherless.

But you take the contract.

Because one-quarter of the profit is 75 ducats. And in seven years as an apprentice, you never earned a single coin. Your master gave you food, a place to sleep, and training. No wages.

This is your first money.

Now you're 25. A journeyman. You don't need a master's roof anymore.

The work changed. No more months at sea. You hire out your skills by the day. Carpentry, most weeks. Three pence a day for standard work. Four if you're fast. Five in London when they're desperate.

Three pence buys two loaves and a room for the night. Before the plague killed half the workers, three pence bought you just the bread. Now it buys more. The masters complain. You don't.

You rent a room above a tavern. Your own door. Your own lock. You eat meat twice a week. You buy a second shirt.

But the room comes with a neighbor. Another journeyman. He works for a Flemish merchant who pays six pence a day and doesn't care about guild rules. The Flemish merchant brings in goods from Antwerp, undercuts local prices, takes contracts the guild says belong to local masters.

Your masters notice. They ask questions. Who's working for outsiders? Who's breaking rates?

You keep your head down. The Flemish merchant's journeyman makes more. But he also knows: one complaint to the guild, and the city watch shuts him down. Confiscates the goods. Maybe worse.

You're making more than your father ever did. But now you're visible.

You start asking: how much does it cost to become a master? How long until you're the one setting the rates, not taking them?

[CH04 | 4:10-5:51 | 成为垄断链条中的一环，获得定价权但导致平民受损，权力方对伤亡虚无化]

You're 30. You're a guild master now.

It took five years. Every florin from those Genoa runs. You borrowed the rest. The entry fee: fifteen weeks of income. You paid.

The guild gives you a seal. Your mark on cloth means it can be sold in this city. Without it, the city watch confiscates. Fines the seller. Sometimes worse.

The guild calls a meeting. You sit with the other masters. Someone says: prices should go up. Everyone nods. You vote. Unanimous.

Cloth prices rise the next week.

At the market, you hear the complaints. A tailor says fabric costs more now. He has to charge customers extra per garment. Customers say they can't afford new clothes. They're making do with old ones.

Someone goes to city hall. Files a complaint. Says the guild is gouging the city.

The city magistrate listens. Then says: this is guild internal business. I don't manage that. He sends them away.

You learn why later. That magistrate was a guild master himself before taking office.

Prices went up. Commoners complained. The official heard nothing.

Your income doubled.

You think about the masterpiece exam you passed. The carved loom shuttle you made to prove your skill. Your father could never have done it. His father couldn't either. But their sons — if they're masters' sons — they skip the exam. Or pay less.

You earned this. That's what you tell yourself.

The system works. For you.

You're 35. Three apprentices. Two journeymen. Your workshop makes decent profit.

One morning you hear noise in the city square. You walk over.

A wooden platform in the center. A man tied to it. You recognize him.

You drank with him two years ago. He paid for the wine.

Now a city crier stands beside him reading from a parchment. Loud enough for the crowd.

The crier lists debts. Names. Amounts. When each debt was made.

"Fled three months ago. Captured in Bristol."

He doesn't look up. His face is bruised.

Behind the platform: his inventory. Bales of wool. Bolts of linen. Tools. Furniture from his house.

The auction starts. City watch stands at each corner. No one moves.

People bid. Low. A competitor buys his best loom for half what it's worth.

The crowd isn't quiet. Someone yells "thief." Someone throws a turnip. It hits his shoulder.

A child near you asks his mother who the man is. She says "someone who didn't pay."

The auction ends.

The crier announces: "The debtor will be held in prison until family or creditors settle the balance."

You watch them untie him. Lead him away.

The crowd disperses. Someone picks up the turnip.

You walk back to your workshop. Your apprentice asks where you went. You don't answer.

That night you count your own debts. The loan you took to expand the workshop. The advance you gave a supplier who hasn't delivered. The guild fees due next month.

The records show a merchant named Veckinchusen was held for three years. Three years in a debtors' cell waiting for someone to pay.

In Florence, the law says it plainly: bankrupt merchants are permanently exiled. Driven from the city. Citizenship stripped. Your children inherit the ban.

He paid for wine two years ago. Now he's in a cell with no window.

The distance between those two moments: one bad shipment. One customer who doesn't pay. One creditor who stops waiting.

You lock the strongbox. Check it twice.

There has to be a way to avoid this. A level where debt doesn't destroy you.

A level where you're the one holding the ledger, not tied to the platform.

What does that level look like?

[CH06 | 7:48-9:53 | 身份彻底改变成为借钱给统治者的债主，债务规模和抵押物等级跃升，但信任瓦解和家庭牺牲]

You're 45. You don't run the goods yourself anymore.

You have twelve agents. Venice. Antwerp. Lyon. Augsburg. Each one does the same thing: lend money to dukes, to princes, sometimes to kings.

1537. Archduke Ferdinand needs 83,000 florins for military supplies. Fourteen percent annual interest. You lend it.

When you lend to royalty, you don't get just interest. You get mines. Trade monopolies. The right to name city magistrates.

But the cost accumulates in a different ledger.

Your daughter turns 15. You're in Antwerp negotiating a 300,000 florin loan. You miss her betrothal feast. She writes you a letter. You read it three months later.

You can't trust partners. You can't trust agents. The numbers in the ledgers are too large. One betrayal, one miscalculation, and you're the one tied to the platform.

You have mines in Spain. Silver from Guadalcanal. Mercury from Almadén. Collateral from kings.

You have everything you could want. You have nothing you actually need.

Your daughter doesn't recognize your handwriting anymore. Your mother's grave has your brother's name on the stone, not yours.

Just his debts to you: 1.25 million florins.

But here's what leverage really looks like.

"It is well known that Your Imperial Majesty could not have acquired the Roman crown without my help."

You're not asking. You're stating a fact. Then you make it clear: pay what you owe, or I stop lending.

But here's what you also know, sitting in that fortified house reading the weekly reports:

The debt is so large now that if he couldn't pay, you'd lose everything. You've lent so much that his collapse would be your collapse.

The same leverage that lets you threaten him also chains you to him.

Leverage works—until the debtor owes more than he can ever repay. Then you can't pull the rope without hanging yourself.

Will this leverage hold? Will the king keep paying?

Or is there a point where the debt gets so large that threatening to stop becomes a threat to yourself?

[CH08 | 11:26-12:13 | 权力彻底反转，最大债务人破产，债主的leverage瞬间失效，从能威胁国王到被锁死的状态]
